messages.author: fe049c2835236bb1
messages.subject: future predictions with colext
parts:
Hello Group,

This may be a very basic question, but for the life of me I cannot find reference to it in any forum post or paper. If I want to make predictions for future years in a dynamic occupancy model, how would I go about that without having to do all the math by hand? I understand I'll need to make some assumptions, like my covariates won't change (I am not using climate and thus cannot rely on GCMs, and I have no future land use models, etc.), and that future species-environment relationships won't change, and probably some more I can't think of right now.

I have data for 2010-2015, and the model returns estimates for psi at 2010-2015, and for col and ext at 2010-2014. This makes sense because the model needs occupancy estimates at 2015 to calculate col and ext at 2014 (right?). So how can calculate psi for 2016 if I don't have col and ext estimates for 2015? How would I go about calculating those?

I'm using the maximum likelihood-based `colext()` function in unmarked, and was wondering if there is a nice way to make future predictions with the available functions. Or is this only viable/tenable using Bayesian methods?

My apologies for the mass of questions. Please be merciful if I'm asking something dumb. Thank you all.

- Jamie

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] future predictions with colext
parts:
If your model uses year as a factor, then you're making no provision to predict outside of the years in your dataset.  (Other than relying on some outside justification that 2016 is just like one of the other years.)

Have you considered treating year not as a factor or letting the other available covariates do the work for estimating col and ext across all years?  That would at least allow a direct prediction for future years.  (You'd still need to do an assessment as to how good such predictions might be.)

Jim

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] future predictions with colext
parts:
Dear Jamie,

there are a couple of ways how you could make such forecasts, and they differ in their degree of sophistication.
(1) You could assume that the year effects that you have estimated are characteristic of the annual variation in the system and write R code that takes occupancy for every site for the last year (2015) and then randomly picks one of the interannual values of colonisation and extinction to produce an estimate of occupancy in 2016. You repeat this 1000 times or so and take the average as your point estimate and the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles as your 95% confidence limits. This you could do directly with the output from your analysis in unmarked.
(2) A better approach would be to fit the model with colonisation and extinction both specified as yearly random effects. When you then predict to 2016, you directly get a posterior distribution of the occupancy forecast. This you would most likely have to do with BUGS.

No doubt there are other methods. The first one is what matrix population modellers sometimes did (at least up to about 15 years ago) in population viability analyses. The latter one is a more elegant solution which is trivial with bayesian MCMC.

If this important to you, then it would be worthwhile to read around how people do such forecasts in other fields of ecology, especially population modeling.

Best regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] future predictions with colext
parts:
You could certainly try using year as a "continuous" covariate rather than as a factor for col and ext.  That would allow the model to predict directly for future years.  Of course, you'd need to examine the AIC values to see if using year in that manner does any better than models without year and you'd need to perform simulations to see if predictions out several years are worth anything.  (With population viability analyses many times predictions of probabilities out several years result in confidence intervals spanning from zero to one which makes predictions out too far being kinda useless.)

And using "year" as a covariate is many times just a proxy for some underlying variable that's more related to the cause of the change.  But using year does have the advantage of being real easy to measure!

Jim

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] future predictions with colext
parts:
Here is something specific when year is treated as a continuous covariate and not as a factor which allows one to make predictions for future years.  What I do is augment the original unmarkedMultFrame with the future covariates and make all of the associated observations NA.  Running colext ignores those missing values for estimation purposes but does construct the predictions for all because the covariates are present.  (Of course, one needs to check model fit and rationalize that future observations are likely to result from at least a similar model.)

Below is an example modified from the vignette "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked" by Marc Kery and Richard Chandler.

# Load library
  library(unmarked)
  
# Simulate some data
  M <- 250 # Number of sites
  J <- 3 # num secondary sample periods
  T <- 10 # num primary sample periods
  psi <- rep(NA, T) # Occupancy probability
  muZ <- z <- array(dim = c(M, T)) # Expected and realized occurrence
  y <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J, T)) # Detection histories
  set.seed(13973)
  psi[1] <- 0.4 # Initial occupancy probability
  p <- rep(0.6,T)
  # Extinction probability:  logit is linear in year
  epsilon <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.1-0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Extinction probability
  phi <- 1 - epsilon
  gamma <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.3+0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Colonization probability
  # Generate latent states of occurrence
  # First year
  z[,1] <- rbinom(M, 1, psi[1]) # Initial occupancy state
# Later years
  for(i in 1:M){ # Loop over sites
     for(k in 2:T){ # Loop over years
        muZ[k] <- z[i, k-1]*phi[k-1] + (1-z[i, k-1])*gamma[k-1]
        z[i,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[k])
     }
  }
# Generate detection/non-detection data
  for(i in 1:M){
     for(k in 1:T){
        prob <- z[i,k] * p[k]
        for(j in 1:J){
           y[i,j,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob)
        } 
     }
  }

# Make unmarkedMultFrame for original data
  yy <- matrix(y, M, J*T)
  year <- matrix(c(1:10), nrow(yy), T, byrow=TRUE)
  simUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy, yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year),
    numPrimary=T)
    
# Analysis before augmenting with "future" observations
  m  <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year, epsilonformula = ~ year,
    pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF, method="BFGS")
  summary(m)
  
# Add columns to yy and year associated with a future year
# Actual values go into year.future and missing values go into yy.future
# (Predictions for multiple future years can also be added here)
  yy.future = cbind(yy,matrix(rep(NA,M*J),nrow=M))
  # Here I've added year T+1 but any other year could be added
  year.future <- cbind(year,matrix(rep(T+1,M),nrow=M))
  simUMF.future <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy.future, 
    yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year.future), numPrimary=T+1)
    
# Run colext on augmented data
  m.future <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year,
    epsilonformula = ~ year, pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF.future, method="BFGS")
  summary(m.future)
  
# Make predictions
  m.fu...@projected.mean
  m.fu...@smoothed.mean

Marc - The first method you described would certainly be a way to use year as predictor and predict into future years, but also comes with assumptions, as you've stated. On Monday, 26 September 2016 03:31:37 UTC-4, Kery Marc wrote:
Dear Jamie,

there are a couple of ways how you could make such forecasts, and they differ in their degree of sophistication.
(1) You could assume that the year effects that you have estimated are characteristic of the annual variation in the system and write R code that takes occupancy for every site for the last year (2015) and then randomly picks one of the interannual values of colonisation and extinction to produce an estimate of occupancy in 2016. You repeat this 1000 times or so and take the average as your point estimate and the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles as your 95% confidence limits. This you could do directly with the output from your analysis in unmarked.
(2) A better approach would be to fit the model with colonisation and extinction both specified as yearly random effects. When you then predict to 2016, you directly get a posterior distribution of the occupancy forecast. This you would most likely have to do with BUGS.

Sent: 26 September 2016 06:46
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [unmarked] future predictions with colext

If your model uses year as a factor, then you're making no provision to predict outside of the years in your dataset.  (Other than relying on some outside justification that 2016 is just like one of the other years.)

Have you considered treating year not as a factor or letting the other available covariates do the work for estimating col and ext across all years?  That would at least allow a direct prediction for future years.  (You'd still need to do an assessment as to how good such predictions might be.)

Jim

This may be a very basic question, but for the life of me I cannot find reference to it in any forum post or paper. - Jamie

On Thursday, 29 September 2016 12:41:39 UTC-4, Jim Baldwin, USDA Forest Service wrote:
Here is something specific when year is treated as a continuous covariate and not as a factor which allows one to make predictions for future years.  What I do is augment the original unmarkedMultFrame with the future covariates and make all of the associated observations NA.  Running colext ignores those missing values for estimation purposes but does construct the predictions for all because the covariates are present.  (Of course, one needs to check model fit and rationalize that future observations are likely to result from at least a similar model.)

Below is an example modified from the vignette "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked" by Marc Kery and Richard Chandler.

# Load library
  library(unmarked)
  
# Simulate some data
  M <- 250 # Number of sites
  J <- 3 # num secondary sample periods
  T <- 10 # num primary sample periods
  psi <- rep(NA, T) # Occupancy probability
  muZ <- z <- array(dim = c(M, T)) # Expected and realized occurrence
  y <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J, T)) # Detection histories
  set.seed(13973)
  psi[1] <- 0.4 # Initial occupancy probability
  p <- rep(0.6,T)
  # Extinction probability:  logit is linear in year
  epsilon <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.1-0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Extinction probability
  phi <- 1 - epsilon
  gamma <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.3+0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Colonization probability
  # Generate latent states of occurrence
  # First year
  z[,1] <- rbinom(M, 1, psi[1]) # Initial occupancy state
# Later years
  for(i in 1:M){ # Loop over sites
     for(k in 2:T){ # Loop over years
        muZ[k] <- z[i, k-1]*phi[k-1] + (1-z[i, k-1])*gamma[k-1]
        z[i,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[k])
     }
  }
# Generate detection/non-detection data
  for(i in 1:M){
     for(k in 1:T){
        prob <- z[i,k] * p[k]
        for(j in 1:J){
           y[i,j,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob)
        } 
     }
  }

# Make unmarkedMultFrame for original data
  yy <- matrix(y, M, J*T)
  year <- matrix(c(1:10), nrow(yy), T, byrow=TRUE)
  simUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy, yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year),
    numPrimary=T)
    
# Analysis before augmenting with "future" observations
  m  <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year, epsilonformula = ~ year,
    pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF, method="BFGS")
  summary(m)
  
# Add columns to yy and year associated with a future year
# Actual values go into year.future and missing values go into yy.future
# (Predictions for multiple future years can also be added here)
  yy.future = cbind(yy,matrix(rep(NA,M*J),nrow=M))
  # Here I've added year T+1 but any other year could be added
  year.future <- cbind(year,matrix(rep(T+1,M),nrow=M))
  simUMF.future <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy.future, 
    yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year.future), numPrimary=T+1)
    
# Run colext on augmented data
  m.future <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year,
    epsilonformula = ~ year, pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF.future, method="BFGS")
  summary(m.future)
  
# Make predictions
  m.fu...@projected.mean
  m.fu...@smoothed.mean

Dear Jamie,

Using random year effects in a Bayesian analysis, it is trivially easy to predict into the future, with the usual full error propagation into these predictions. We have an example of this in chapter 5 on state-space models in our BPA book (you can download the code from the book web site).

Sent: 28 September 2016 18:32

Subject: Re: [unmarked] future predictions with colext

You could certainly try using year as a "continuous" covariate rather than as a factor for col and ext.  That would allow the model to predict directly for future years.  Of course, you'd need to examine the AIC values to see if using year in that manner does any better than models without year and you'd need to perform simulations to see if predictions out several years are worth anything.  (With population viability analyses many times predictions of probabilities out several years result in confidence intervals spanning from zero to one which makes predictions out too far being kinda useless.)

And using "year" as a covariate is many times just a proxy for some underlying variable that's more related to the cause of the change.  But using year does have the advantage of being real easy to measure!

Jim
